claims.claim: Jupiter is the biggest planet in the solar system.
claims.source_checked: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/
claims.note: Fact sheet: Jupiter has the largest mass (1898e24 kg) and diameter (142,984 km) of the eight planets.

claims.claim: Two and a half times the mass of every other planet combined.
claims.source_checked: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/

claims.claim: JUPITER / 2.5× the other planets combined, by mass
claims.source_checked: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/
claims.note: Same figures as n=2; 2.47 → 2.5×, and 'by mass' scopes it correctly.

claims.claim: Row of the other seven planets beneath Jupiter at one scale (96 units per Jupiter radius): Saturn 0.833, Uranus 0.363, Neptune 0.352, Earth 0.091, Venus 0.087, Mars 0.0485, Mercury 0.035
claims.source_checked: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/ (index) and https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/jupiterfact.html, https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/saturnfact.html, https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/uranusfact.html, https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/neptunefact.html, https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/earthfact.html, https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/venusfact.html, https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/marsfact.html, https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/mercuryfact.html
claims.note: The drawn ratios are right: the volumetric mean radii on the individual fact sheets (69,911; 58,232; 25,362; 24,622; 6,371; 6,051.8; 3,389.5; 2,439.7 km) give 0.833, 0.363, 0.352, 0.091, 0.087, 0.0485, 0.035. But SOURCES 11 cites the 'NASA Planetary Fact Sheet, same page as claim 1'. That index page lists diameters, not volumetric mean radii. Change only the citation in SOURCES 11 to the per-planet fact sheets (…/factsheet/<planet>fact.html). The visual needs no change.

claims.claim: But hold Jupiter up next to the Sun, and it looks tiny.
claims.source_checked: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/sunfact.html, https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/jupiterfact.html
claims.note: Volumetric mean radius 695,700 km against 69,911 km, a ratio of 9.95: Jupiter is about a tenth of the Sun's width. 'Looks tiny' is a fair description.

claims.claim: Jupiter shrinks to radius 26 as the Sun rises and fills the frame (Sun drawn at radius 520, then settles at 330)
claims.source_checked: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/sunfact.html, https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/jupiterfact.html
claims.note: To scale, the Sun is 9.95 Jupiter radii. As drawn it is 520/26 = 20 and then 330/26 = 12.7, so Jupiter is shown 2× and then 1.28× too small, right on the line 'it looks tiny', with no not-to-scale notice (A6). Fix: draw Jupiter at about 52 while the Sun is 520 and at 33 once it settles at 330 (or the Sun at 259 against a Jupiter of 26). Otherwise, label the shot as not to scale.

claims.claim: It would take nearly a thousand Jupiters to fill the Sun.
claims.source_checked: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/sunfact.html, https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/jupiterfact.html
claims.note: Sun volume 1,412,000e12 km³; Jupiter 143,128e10 = 1,431.28e12 km³; ratio 986.5, so 'nearly a thousand' holds by volume. A pedant could object that solid spheres pack worse (roughly 600 rigid Jupiters would fit). SOURCES records this, and 'fill' read as volume is what the fact sheet supports.

claims.claim: ≈ 1,000 JUPITERS / to fill it
claims.source_checked: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/sunfact.html, https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/jupiterfact.html
claims.note: 986.5 ≈ 1,000; matches the spoken line. (The dot visual under it is n=9.)

claims.claim: 1,000 small dots spread evenly across the Sun's disc out to its edge
claims.source_checked: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/sunfact.html, https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/jupiterfact.html
claims.note: A 2-D disc of the Sun holds only about 99 Jupiter-sized discs by area (9.95²). For 1,000 dots to tile the disc, each must have about 1/33 of the Sun's radius, but Jupiter is 1/9.95. So the dots show Jupiter about 3× too small, right after Jupiter was drawn beside the Sun. The 'fill' is a volume claim that a flat disc cannot show at scale. A6 requires the visual to say so: add an on-screen note such as 'by volume' and 'dots not to scale' (or make the sub 'by volume'), or show the fill in a way that does not read as Jupiter-sized discs.

claims.claim: Our Sun is not an average star. It is an unusually big one.
claims.source_checked: Reylé et al. 2021, doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202140985 (Crossref record) read via arXiv:2104.14972v2 full text: abstract, Table 3, Sect. 3.5
claims.note: Table 3 (Sun excluded): A 4, F 8, G 18, K 38, M 249, white dwarfs (D) 20, N/A 41. Even if all A, F and G stars are counted as bigger, the Sun sits in the top ~10% by size within 10 pc.

claims.claim: It is bigger and brighter than over ninety percent of the stars in our part of the galaxy
claims.source_checked: Reylé et al. 2021, doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202140985 (Crossref record) read via arXiv:2104.14972v2 full text: abstract, Table 3, Sect. 3.5
claims.note: The claim holds, but the margin is thinner than SOURCES says. SOURCES 4 treats every K star as a dwarf, smaller and dimmer than the Sun. Reylé Sect. 3.5 lists four evolved subgiants within 10 pc: β Hyi, µ Her Aa, δ Pav and δ Eri. δ Eri is a K-type subgiant, generally K0 IV, larger and more luminous than the Sun. I could not open the CDS Table A.1 to confirm its type there. Worst case (all A, F, G and δ Eri counted as at least the Sun): smaller = 37 K + 249 M + 20 D = 306 of 337 typed stars = 90.8%. With the 36 possible M stars and 1 possible WD among the untyped, 343/374 = 91.7%. 'Over ninety percent' survives. Recommend correcting SOURCES 4 to note δ Eri and the 90.8% floor.

claims.claim: THE SUN / bigger than 9 stars in 10
claims.source_checked: Reylé et al. 2021, doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202140985 (Crossref record) read via arXiv:2104.14972v2 full text: abstract, Table 3, Sect. 3.5
claims.note: Floor 90.8% (see n=11) ≥ 9 in 10.

claims.claim: because most stars are red dwarfs: small, dim, and everywhere.
claims.source_checked: Reylé et al. 2021, doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202140985 (Crossref record) read via arXiv:2104.14972v2 full text: abstract, Table 3, Sect. 3.5
claims.note: M stars are 249/337 = 74% of typed stars. The paper gives 58.9 ± 5.8% of all typed objects including brown dwarfs, and about 61% including estimated types. That is a majority on every reading. Two loose points: 'everywhere' is figurative (the census is local), and the 90% also relies on K dwarfs and white dwarfs, so red dwarfs are the main reason, not the only one. Neither makes the line false.

claims.claim: 10×10 grid of 100 dots: 5 large bright yellow (≥ Sun), 10 orange (K), 3 smaller yellow (G smaller than Sun), 5 tiny white (white dwarfs), 77 red (M), presented as census proportion
claims.source_checked: Reylé et al. 2021, doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202140985 (Crossref record) read via arXiv:2104.14972v2 full text: abstract, Table 3, Sect. 3.5
claims.note: (1) The grid does not match its stated basis. SOURCES 9 uses ~375 stars (337 typed + Sun + 37 untyped stellar). On that basis M = 249+36 = 285 → 76.0%, and white dwarfs = 20+1 = 21 → 5.6%, so the dots should be 76 red and 6 white, not 77 and 5. On the typed-only basis (338) it is 74 red, 11 K, 6 white. (2) The 5 large / 3 small-G split depends on 'about a third of the 18 G stars' being at least the Sun's size. That has no A2 citation: Reylé gives only spectral classes, not radii. Depending on the G split, the true 'at least the Sun' share runs from 13/375 (3.5%) to 32/375 (8.5%). Fix: cite per-star radii for the 18 G stars (and δ Eri, which belongs in the 'large' group), or recount from them. At minimum, change to 76 red / 6 white.

claims.claim: THE SUN / one of the five
claims.where: on-screen: tag as the Sun joins the 5 large dots
claims.source_checked: Reylé et al. 2021, doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202140985 (Crossref record) read via arXiv:2104.14972v2 full text: abstract, Table 3, Sect. 3.5
claims.note: 'Five' in 100 rests on the unsourced G-star split in n=14. It is plausible, but no cited source gives the radii of the 18 G stars, and the honest range is about 3.5–8.5%. Source the split, or make the label not depend on an exact count.

claims.claim: So look at the nearest star to our own. … The closest star to the Sun
claims.source_checked: Anglada-Escudé et al. 2016, Nature 536, 437, doi:10.1038/nature19106 (Crossref record; text read via arXiv:1609.03449, the accepted version; nature.com refused the proxy)
claims.note: Abstract: 'At a distance of 1.295 parsecs, the red-dwarf Proxima Centauri … is the Sun's closest stellar neighbour'. The script correctly says 'closest star to the Sun', not to us.

claims.claim: Proxima Centauri, just over four light years away.
claims.source_checked: NASA Exoplanet Archive TAP, pscomppars + stellarhosts where hostname like 'Proxima%' (sy_dist, sy_vmag, st_spectype, st_rad, st_rad_reflink); Anglada-Escudé et al. 2016 (arXiv:1609.03449)
claims.note: Archive sy_dist 1.30119 ± 0.00034 pc = 4.244 ly; Nature 1.295 pc = 4.22 ly. Both are 'just over four'. SOURCES also cites Gaia DR3 (doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202243940) for 4.2465 ly. That DOI is the DR3 summary paper (Vallenari et al. 2023, A&A 674, A1), which does not itself give Proxima's parallax, so it is not a source for that figure. It is not needed; drop it or cite the DR3 catalogue entry.

claims.claim: The closest star to the Sun, and you have almost certainly never seen it. It is almost always too faint for your eyes.
claims.source_checked: NASA Exoplanet Archive TAP, pscomppars + stellarhosts where hostname like 'Proxima%' (sy_dist, sy_vmag, st_spectype, st_rad, st_rad_reflink); Howard et al. 2018, ApJL 860, L30, doi:10.3847/2041-8213/aacaf3 (publisher abstract via Crossref)
claims.note: Archive V = 11.01. Howard et al.: 'the Evryscope observed the first naked-eye-brightness superflare detected from Proxima Centauri … increased in optical flux by a factor of ∼68'. That directly supports 'almost always too faint' and the 'almost' hedge. I could not open Schaefer 1993 (doi:10.1016/0083-6656(93)90113-X): ScienceDirect returned a bot check, and ADS a verification wall. So the 'magnitude 6' limit and '100 times too faint' in SOURCES 7 are not confirmed by me. They are not spoken.

claims.claim: PROXIMA CENTAURI / ≈ 0.15× the Sun's radius (drawn at radius 14.4 against the Sun at 96)
claims.source_checked: Kervella et al. 2017, A&A 598, L7, doi:10.1051/0004-6361/201629930 (Crossref; full text arXiv:1611.03495); NASA Exoplanet Archive TAP, pscomppars + stellarhosts where hostname like 'Proxima%' (sy_dist, sy_vmag, st_spectype, st_rad, st_rad_reflink)
claims.note: Kervella: 'RProx = 0.1542±0.0045 R☉' (Table 1). Archive adopts 0.141 ± 0.021 (reflink Suárez Mascareño et al. 2025, 2025A&A...700A..11M). 0.15 lies inside both ranges, and 14.4/96 = 0.150.

claims.claim: That is what most of the stars around us look like. (5 large bright dots fade out)
claims.source_checked: Reylé et al. 2021, doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202140985 (Crossref record) read via arXiv:2104.14972v2 full text: abstract, Table 3, Sect. 3.5; NASA Exoplanet Archive TAP, pscomppars + stellarhosts where hostname like 'Proxima%' (sy_dist, sy_vmag, st_spectype, st_rad, st_rad_reflink)
claims.note: Proxima is M5.5 V (archive), and M dwarfs are 74% of typed stars within 10 pc. Note: SOURCES 8 calls a mid-M dwarf 'the typical star' using the paper's 'M3.0 V to M5.0 V' bin, but Proxima (M5.5) falls just outside that bin. Rest the line on the M-dwarf majority, not on that quote.

claims.claim: The star we call ordinary is one of the rare big ones.
claims.source_checked: Reylé et al. 2021, doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202140985 (Crossref record) read via arXiv:2104.14972v2 full text: abstract, Table 3, Sect. 3.5
claims.note: Even the widest reading (A 4 + F 8 + all 18 G + δ Eri + Sun = 32 of ~375, or 32/338 = 9.5%) leaves stars at least the Sun's size under 10%, so 'rare' holds whichever way the G stars split.

claims.claim: Hook, first sentence alone: 'Jupiter is the biggest planet in the solar system.'
claims.source_checked: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/
claims.note: True as stated. A viewer who swipes at second two leaves with a true fact. The surprising claim (the Sun is unusually big) is corrective, not a false popular version.
